item.title: Death toll unknown after Dutch tour bus crashes in Switzerland
item.description:
Death toll unknown after Dutch tour bus crashes in Switzerland

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of fatalities from a serious accident involving a Dutch tour bus travelling through Switzerland is still not known.

The vehicle had 48 passengers and one driver on board when it crashed between the villages of Susch and Zernez in eastern Switzerland on Thursday afternoon, broadcaster NOS reported.

Swiss police have confirmed that several people have died and more were injured, but must notify next of kin before making a public announcement. Emergency services spent the evening recovering the bodies.

Swiss president Guy Parmelin said on social media he was “deeply shocked and dismayed” by the accident. “At this painful time, my thoughts are with the victims and their loved ones. I offer my sincere condolences to the families of those who lost their lives,” he said.

Dutch travel company Oad organised the trip, and the bus is owned by Hartemink, a coach firm from Eibergen in Gelderland. The group was on a tour of Austria and had taken a day trip to Switzerland. Swiss authorities have said they believe most, if not all, of the passengers are Dutch.

The cause of the accident is also not known. Swiss police told local media that no other vehicles were involved and that the crash happened at a stretch of roadworks where the lanes had been narrowed. The bus went through the crash barrier and overturned.

Local police have opened an emergency number for anyone who may have family on board: +41 81 256 56 56.

item.title: Amsterdam artists behind 9/11 drone tribute in New York
item.description:
Amsterdam artists behind 9/11 drone tribute in New York

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

An Amsterdam art collective and a Dutch designer were behind the memorial light installation for the Twin Towers in New York on Wednesday night, two days before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks.

Exactly 2,977 drones – one for every person killed in the attacks – were flown over New York Harbor to form the outline of the two skyscrapers. The display, titled “2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor”, appeared twice for 15 minutes each time.

Amsterdam studio Drift, which has also used drones to rebuild landmarks such as Rome’s Colosseum in light, acted as artistic advisor on the project, alongside Japanese architect Shigeru Ban.

The show itself was designed by Yan Paul Dubbelman, a Dutch digital artist also based in Amsterdam. American creative director Addison Mehr led the project, which was developed with relatives of victims, survivors, and first responders.

Drift co-founder Ralph Nauta told broadcaster NOS the idea came to him while walking through New York two years ago. The aim was to give those who had lost someone “something beautiful with light”, he said. “It is of course very emotional for everyone who lost someone there to see the Twin Towers again.”

The drones were not allowed to fly on the eve of the anniversary itself for security reasons, NOS reported, so the show took place a day earlier. It was designed to sit alongside Tribute in Light, the two beams projected from Lower Manhattan every year on September 11.

Friday’s official ceremony at the 9/11 Memorial in Manhattan takes place under the heaviest security in years, with relatives reading out the names of all the victims. For the first time, the roughly 9,000 people who have since died of illnesses linked to the attacks will also be commemorated.

item.title: Four people with long Covid euthanised in NL last year
item.description:
Four people with long Covid euthanised in NL last year

September 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Four people died by euthanasia last year after suffering with long Covid, according to the Dutch regional euthanasia review committee.

The youngest patient was 51-years-old, the other three were over 65. In another six cases, long Covid played a role in the decision to end their lives but was not the primary factor.

An estimated 400,000 people in the Netherlands currently suffer from long Covid, many of them have severe symptoms that stop them working or being able to enjoy basic everyday activities.

The Dutch Health Council this year urged the government to give more clarity around the situation with long Covid and do more to help treat those suffering from it.

Last month, a national research and investigation centre was launched by the Long-Covid Foundation, to help prolong work into treating the illness.

Government funding of €40 million dried up, so the foundation raised €500,000 to give to seven scientists to keep researching possible treatments.

item.title: Roof of PM’s office is original 16th-century flat-plack
item.description:
Roof of PM’s office is original 16th-century flat-plack

September 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The roof of the Torentje, or Little Tower, at the Binnenhof in The Hague was built in 1547 as a construction kit and has been largely untouched since, broadcaster NOS reported on Thursday.

The research on the eight-metre-high spire above the office of the prime minister was carried out by the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf, the government’s property agency, during the ongoing renovation of the complex.

The ceiling was opened last year to check the area for asbestos, which was found, revealing the oak roof structure behind it.

The wooden construction has needed practically no repair work in 478 years.
An inspection revealed that the beams were sawn by hand, typical in the days before the widespread use of sawmills. The wood came from an oak tree felled in southern Sweden around 1546.

Roman numerals are also chiselled into the beams, indicating that the roof was built in a workshop, taken apart and transported to the building site. The numerals show which parts belong together, like the instructions for a piece of Ikea furniture.

The tower itself is older: the earliest records date from 1497, and Emperor Charles V had it completely rebuilt in 1547, when the spire was added.

The renovation of the Binnenhof began in 2021. The work was initially expected to take five years and cost €475 million, but the bill has since risen to at least €2.7 billion and completion has been postponed until 2031.

Earlier this year, archaeologists found an early 14th-century city gate at the site.

item.title: Parents as “customers” fuelling school disputes, council says
item.description:
Parents as “customers” fuelling school disputes, council says

September 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Parents are falling out with schools and turning to dispute committees to settle grievances, according to the the government’s independent education council. This is happening partly because parents are being turned into “customers” of the education system, where they can publicly compare and select schools.

The council was asked to look into the problem by the former education minister and sent its findings on Thursday.

Tension between parents and schools is usually blamed on social media, polarisation and a more individualistic society, it said, but that explanation leaves out the part played by law and policy in setting the two sides against each other.

Policy changes, such as the 2014 passend onderwijs reform, which leaves parents and schools to agree between themselves when a child qualifies for additional support, have raised tensions. Previously, an outside committee would make these decisions.

Websites allowing parents to compare schools on performance data, such as exam pass rates and the share of pupils recommended for pre-university education, have also created a customer and provider dynamic, the report said.

Disputes taken to the national dispute committees for schools rose steadily until 2024, with a slight dip last year. The number of secondary teachers who say dealing with parents is giving them stress is rising, and in primary schools a third of all teachers say the same.

The council’s two main recommendations are that ministers should consider what a policy will do to the relationship between parents and schools before introducing it, and that parents should be given more say collectively rather than only as individuals with a complaint.

item.title: Calves shipped from Ireland go 50 hours without milk, NVWA says
item.description:
Calves shipped from Ireland go 50 hours without milk, NVWA says

September 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch food and product safety authority NVWA is taking enforcement action against four Irish livestock transporters over the treatment of very young calves shipped to the Netherlands, broadcaster NOS reported on Thursday.

The calves are given almost nothing to drink during a journey of at least 50 hours, which breaches EU animal welfare rules, the NVWA said. The transporters have been given a year to change their working methods or face financial penalties.

The animals, mostly bull calves under two months old, are loaded onto trucks in Ireland and put on a ferry to France. After a 19-hour crossing they are unloaded to rest and drink, then driven on to the Netherlands.

EU rules say animals must be fed during transport where “necessary”, which the European Commission and the NVWA interpret as at least every 12 hours. The Irish authorities disagree and have not intervened.

According to the NVWA, the trucks have no drinking systems suitable for milk, and calves of this age have to be helped to drink. The Irish government has itself said that is “practically impossible” on the ferry.

“That means the animals can no longer go directly from Ireland via France to the Netherlands in one go,” NVWA inspector Annebeth van Aartsen told NOS. “The transport would have to be organised differently.”

The Dutch veal sector said earlier it wanted to stop the Irish imports in 2026 because of the suffering involved, but a NOS investigation this year found the transports were still going on.

The NVWA had previously said it could not act because most of the violations take place at sea, outside Dutch jurisdiction. The action follows an enforcement request by animal welfare groups Eyes on Animals and Dier&Recht.

item.title: Amsterdam fails to get EU backing to limit Airbnb rules
item.description:
Amsterdam fails to get EU backing to limit Airbnb rules

September 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema has failed to persuade the European Commission to help crack down on people renting out their own homes to tourists.

Halsema travelled to Brussels in the spring with the mayors of other big European cities that struggle with mass tourism – like Barcelona and Paris – to lobby for tougher powers to regulate holiday rentals through sites like Airbnb.

But the EU Affordable Housing Act, presented on Wednesday, would not ban or limit holiday lets but instead establishes a standard for when an area is under “housing stress” – defined as one where house prices are at least eight times per capita disposable income and have risen over the past decade.

It then gives local authorities a legal basis to restrict commercial short-term rentals and second-home purchases in those areas.

Combating local damage
Amsterdam had asked the commission for two things, according to the Telegraaf: more powers to act against people letting out the home they live in, and for the right to intervene once an area’s liveability has been damaged by tourist rentals.

The commission seemingly dismissed both requests. The text of the act explicitly excludes a host’s primary residence from any restriction, on the grounds that renting out your own home does not take housing off the market. It also only covers measures justified by affordability and availability, not neighbourhood nuisance.

“It is questionable whether this proposal is going to help us,” Amsterdam housing alderman Zita Pels told the paper. Dirk Gotink, an MEP for the centre-right NSC, also told the Telegraaf: “we don’t need a European law to solve local problems.”

Amsterdam already restricts renting your own home through sites like Airbnb to 30 nights per year but has tried to go further in the past. In July 2020 the council banned holiday rentals outright in the red light district and part of the canal ring.

The Amsterdam district court overturned that ban in 2021, and the Council of State, the highest administrative court, upheld the ruling in 2023, saying a total ban was disproportionate and the city should first have tested less drastic measures, such as a lower night limit.

For people in the Netherlands with a second home in Spain, Portugal or France, nothing will change for now. The law would allow local authorities in stressed areas to restrict purchases of homes not used as a primary residence, but only for property bought after the measure takes effect.

The proposal must first be negotiated by the European Parliament and member states, a process likely to take a year or more.

item.title: Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite
item.description:
Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite

September 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Exports from the Netherlands to the United States fell by 25% in the first half of this year, knocking the US out of the top five destinations for Dutch goods.

Dutch companies sold €13 billion worth of goods to the US between January and June, €4.3 billion less than in the same period last year, figures from national statistics office CBS show. The decline began after the Trump administration imposed a general import tariff of 15% on goods from the EU in August last year.

Almost every type of product was affected. Machinery and transport equipment, the biggest category of Dutch exports to the US, accounted for nearly half the fall. Sales of medicines and other chemical products dropped by more than 30%, and manufactured goods such as medical instruments fell by almost a quarter.

As a result, the US now takes 4% of Dutch goods exports, down from 5.5% a year earlier. Italy has overtaken it as the fifth-biggest market, with Spain also catching up. Exports to Belgium, Germany, France, Spain and Italy all rose over the same period.

Trade in the other direction has grown – imports from the US were up 19% to €27.6 billion, although most of that increase was oil and other fuels, which have become more expensive because of the conflict in the Middle East. Other kinds of imports rose by 6.7%.

The tariffs have been costly for the US as well. The country’s Supreme Court ruled in February that most of the levies Donald Trump introduced last year were illegal, and Dutch companies are now claiming back more than €1 billion in duties.

Philips has already received €186 million, and Heineken and Ahold Delhaize are expected to recover hundreds of millions between them.

In 2024, before the tariffs were introduced, the Netherlands exported more than €38 billion worth of goods to the US, nearly 6% of all its exports.

item.title: Library membership tops 3.8 million as more adults sign up
item.description:
Library membership tops 3.8 million as more adults sign up

September 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More than 3.8 million people were members of public libraries in the Netherlands in 2025, a 3% increase over the year before according to new numbers by national statistics office CBS.

The number of adult library members rose by 46,000 to nearly 1.4 million.

In particular, an increasing number of younger adults, those between the ages of 18 and 30, are joining libraries.

In total, 9% of adults are library members. That statistic is dwarfed by the number of children who are library members. Nearly two-thirds of kids, 74%, are members of a library.

The number of children joining a library has also increased in 2025. Last year saw a rise of 2.4%, or over 57,000 more kids with a library card.

The Netherlands had 802 library locations in 2025, an increase of 35 on the year before. This is due to an increase in funding from the national government, according to CBS.

The number of physical books checked out by patrons has remained stable but the number of e-book loans rose. Nearly 6 million e-books were borrowed via the online library, 3% more than in 2024, and audiobook loans rose 11% to 2.9 million.

item.title: Body of man who fell off boat in Amsterdam found
item.description:
Body of man who fell off boat in Amsterdam found

September 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Divers have recovered the body of a man who fell out of a boat in the IJ in Amsterdam on Wednesday.

The 47-year old went overboard near the Schellingwouderbrug, which connects Amsterdam East and Amsterdam Noord, at around 12:30PM, the regional safety board reported.

Multiple diving teams and rescue boats were dispatched as well as a helicopter equipped with a thermal camera.

After an hour of searching, the operation was scaled back as it was unlikely the man would be found alive.

Divers found his body late Wednesday evening.

It is not clear how the man ended up in the water. The police are investigating.
